title: Why projects have a life cycle
blurb: What a life cycle is, how phases and decision gates control a project, and why every project needs one.
question: A sponsor asks why her new booking website must stop for a formal review between each phase instead of simply carrying on. What are these reviews, and how does splitting the project into phases help her?

teach.h: Every project has a start, a middle and an end
teach.body: A project life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through from start to finish. In plain English: it is the project's roadmap, cut into manageable chunks. Each phase has its own purpose and outputs, and between phases there is a checkpoint called a decision gate. Because projects are temporary, a life cycle always has a defined beginning and a defined end.

steps.label: Phase 1
steps.sub: Do the work this phase needs

steps.label: Phase 2
steps.sub: Plan or build the next layer of detail

steps.label: Phase 3
steps.sub: Deliver the next set of outputs

teach.caption: Phases do the work. Gates decide whether the project has earned the right to carry on.

teach.body: A decision gate is a point between phases where the continuation of the project is decided by the sponsor or governance board. They review the business case, progress so far and readiness for the next phase. The usual outcomes are go, no-go, hold or re-plan. Gates are a governance control: they stop unviable projects early, before more money and effort are committed.

teach.h: What can happen at a gate

root.label: Decision gate review
root.sub: Is the business case still valid? Are we ready?

teach.caption: The decision belongs to the sponsor or governance board, not the delivery team.

items: Structure: a big, uncertain piece of work is broken into manageable phases.
Control points: gates let the sponsor confirm the business case before releasing more funding.
A common language: everyone knows what 'Definition' or 'Deployment' means.
Planning in stages: detail is added as more is known, rather than guessed on day one.
Early exit: a project that no longer makes sense can be stopped before costs grow.

teach.h: The two families of phase names
teach.caption: Hybrid life cycles mix the two. Extended life cycles add Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.

teach.body: Harbourside Council wants online parking permits. In Concept, the idea and an outline business case pass the first gate. In Definition, detailed requirements and plans reveal the cost has doubled. At the gate, the sponsor and board compare that against the benefits and decide no-go. Without a gate, the council would have discovered the problem halfway through the build, with far more money already spent.

teach.h: A linear project with its gates
teach.caption: Illustrative timings. Each gate is a decision point between two phases.

teach.text: A decision gate is not a progress meeting or a sprint review. It sits BETWEEN phases and decides whether the project continues. Also, a gate is a governance decision for the sponsor or board: the project manager prepares for it but does not make the go or no-go call.

items: A life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through from start to finish.
Phases are separated by decision gates: go, no-go, hold or re-plan.
Gates are decided by the sponsor or governance board, using the business case.
Benefits: structure, control points, a common language and early exit from bad projects.
Linear phases: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Iterative: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment.

summary: You can now define a project life cycle, explain how decision gates between phases give the sponsor control, and list why a phased approach helps. You have also met both sets of phase names, linear and iterative, ready for the next lessons.

A.q: Which of the following best defines a project life cycle?
options: The list of tasks taken from the WBS
The series of phases from start to finish
The period in which benefits are measured
The approval route for each change request
A.why: A project life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through from its start to its finish.

whyNot.0: Tasks from the work breakdown structure describe the work, not the phases the whole project passes through.
whyNot.2: Measuring benefits happens in benefits realisation, which is only one part of an extended life cycle.
whyNot.3: Change requests go through change control, which is a separate process.

A.q: What normally separates one phase of a project life cycle from the next?
A.why: Phases are separated by decision gates, where the sponsor or board decides whether the project should continue.

whyNot.0: A time box is a fixed period used inside iterative development, not a boundary between phases.
whyNot.1: A work package is a unit of work within the WBS.
whyNot.3: A sprint review happens at the end of an iteration inside development, not between life cycle phases.

A.q: Who normally makes the go or no-go decision at a decision gate?
options: The members of the project team
The end users of the outputs
A.why: Gate decisions are a governance control made by the sponsor or the governance board, which the sponsor usually chairs.

whyNot.1: Team members carry out the work; they don't authorise the project to continue.
whyNot.2: End users give requirements and accept outputs, but they don't make gate decisions.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports and assures; it doesn't replace the sponsor's authority.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are benefits of using a project life cycle?
1) It gives control points for go or no-go decisions
2) It removes the need for a business case
3) It gives everyone a common language
4) It guarantees the project finishes on time
B.why: A life cycle provides control points (gates) and a shared vocabulary for the phases.

whyNot.0: The business case is still needed: gates use it to decide whether to continue.
whyNot.1: Neither is true: the business case remains essential and no structure can guarantee on-time delivery.
whyNot.2: A common language is a benefit, but no life cycle can guarantee finishing on time.

B.q: At a decision gate, the board finds the project's costs have doubled and the benefits no longer justify it. What is the most appropriate outcome?
options: Go, and review the costs later
Skip ahead to the final phase
Hand the decision to the team
B.why: If the business case is no longer viable, a no-go decision stops the project before more money is committed. That is exactly what gates are for.

whyNot.0: Carrying on when the business case has failed wastes money; gates exist to prevent this.
whyNot.2: Skipping phases doesn't fix an unviable business case.
whyNot.3: Gate decisions belong to the sponsor or board, not the delivery team.

B.q: Which statement about decision gates is correct?
options: They happen inside each time box
They sit between life cycle phases
They only happen at project closure
B.why: Decision gates sit at the boundaries between phases, where continuation of the project is decided.

whyNot.0: Time boxes belong inside iterative development; gates sit between the phases of the life cycle.
whyNot.1: A gate reviews the plan and business case; it doesn't replace them.
whyNot.3: Gates occur between every phase, not just at the end.

C.q: A sponsor likes that her project is split into phases because she does not have to commit the full budget on day one. Which benefit of a life cycle is she describing?
options: Funding is released phase by phase
Risks are removed by the first gate
The team plans every task on day one
C.why: Gates let the sponsor commit money and resources one phase at a time, after confirming the business case is still valid.

whyNot.1: Phasing doesn't freeze scope at Concept; detail is added as the project progresses.
whyNot.2: No gate removes all risk; it checks that remaining risks are acceptable.
whyNot.3: A phased life cycle does the opposite: detail is planned progressively as more is known.

C.q: A project manager says: 'We'll plan every task in full detail on day one, so we don't need phases.' Which weakness in this view does a life cycle address?
options: Plans must be approved by the end users
Phases remove the need for estimating
Detail is only known as work progresses
C.why: Early on, much is uncertain. A life cycle adds detail phase by phase as understanding grows, and gates check the plan at each step.

whyNot.0: Plans are approved by the sponsor, and that isn't the weakness being described.
whyNot.1: Estimating is still needed in every phase; it just becomes more accurate later.
whyNot.2: Gates don't replace planning; they review it.

C.q: Which statement about project life cycles is NOT correct?
options: Phases are separated by decision gates
A life cycle runs from start to finish
Every project must use the linear model
C.why: There is no single compulsory model: linear, iterative, hybrid and extended life cycles each suit different situations.

whyNot.0: True: the right model depends on the project, especially how stable its requirements are.
whyNot.1: True: decision gates separate the phases.
whyNot.2: True: a life cycle covers the project from start to finish.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You want a kitchen extension. Would you pay the builder in full before an architect had even drawn it? How do phases and gates protect you?

blocks.h: You commit a bit at a time
blocks.body: First you check the idea is affordable and worth it. Then you pay an architect for drawings and get firm quotes. Only then do builders start, and finally you check the work and move in. Before each step you pause and ask: still worth it? Still affordable? That pause is a decision gate. If the quotes come back far too high, you stop, having spent only a little.

blocks.h: The extension as a life cycle

blocks.text: The gate is the pause and decision BETWEEN steps, not the step itself. The person paying (the sponsor) makes that call.

explain.body: A project life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through from start to finish. Each phase has a clear purpose and outputs, so the project is easier to plan, manage and talk about.

test.q: Complete the statement: a project life cycle is the series of ___ a project passes through from start to finish.
test.why: A life cycle is made up of phases, separated by decision gates.

whyNot.0: Tasks are the detailed activities inside the phases.
whyNot.1: Risks are managed throughout; they don't make up the life cycle.
whyNot.3: Reports communicate progress; they aren't the stages of the project.

explain.body: Between phases, the sponsor or governance board reviews the business case, progress and readiness, then decides: go, no-go, hold or re-plan. This stops unviable projects early.

test.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate?
options: To decide if the project continues
To assign work packages to the team
To fix scope for the whole project
test.why: A decision gate decides whether the project should continue into the next phase.

whyNot.1: Allocating work is day-to-day project management, not a gate decision.
whyNot.2: Lessons are captured in a post-project review.
whyNot.3: Fixing scope is part of baselining in a linear life cycle, not the purpose of every gate.

explain.body: A life cycle gives structure, control points, a common language and the chance to plan in stages. Money and effort are committed one phase at a time, so a failing project can be stopped before costs grow.

test.q: Which of the following is a benefit of using a project life cycle?
options: It fixes the budget at Concept
test.why: A life cycle gives everyone a common language, as well as structure and control points.

whyNot.0: No life cycle removes all risk.
whyNot.2: The sponsor is central: they make the gate decisions.
whyNot.3: Budgets are refined as the project progresses; early estimates are ranges.

explain.body: Linear: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Iterative: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment. Learn both lists and their order: the exam tests them heavily.

test.q: Which set of phase names belongs to the linear life cycle?
test.why: The linear life cycle runs Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition.

whyNot.1: These are the iterative phases (with Evolutionary development).
whyNot.2: This mixes linear, iterative and extended names.
whyNot.3: Feasibility is iterative and Closure is not a phase name in the linear model.
